final_proof:
Proof. Since X and Y take values in the natural numbers, extend their mass functions to all nonnegative integers by putting p_k = Pr(X = k) and q_k = Pr(Y = k), with probability zero for any k outside the corresponding codomain. Their probability generating functions are therefore

Π_X(s) = ∑_{k=0}^∞ p_k s^k  and  Π_Y(s) = ∑_{k=0}^∞ q_k s^k.

For every s with |s| ≤ 1 these series converge absolutely, because ∑ p_k |s|^k ≤ ∑ p_k = 1, and similarly for q_k. (As usual, the constant monomial s^0 is 1, also at s = 0.)

Suppose first that p_k = q_k for every k. Then the two absolutely convergent series have equal corresponding terms, so Π_X(s) = Π_Y(s) for every s ∈ [-1,1].

Conversely, suppose Π_X(s) = Π_Y(s) for every s ∈ [-1,1]. Set a_k = p_k - q_k. Absolute convergence permits subtraction of the two series, and hence

∑_{k=0}^∞ a_k s^k = 0

for every 0 < s < 1. Moreover,

∑_{k=0}^∞ |a_k| ≤ ∑_{k=0}^∞ (p_k + q_k) = 2.

We prove by induction that a_k = 0 for every k ≥ 0. For k = 0, the displayed power-series identity gives

0 = a_0 + ∑_{k=1}^∞ a_k s^k.

The absolute value of its tail is at most

∑_{k=1}^∞ |a_k|s^k ≤ s∑_{k=1}^∞ |a_k| ≤ 2s.

Letting s decrease to 0 therefore yields a_0 = 0. Now let n ≥ 1 and suppose a_0 = ⋯ = a_{n-1} = 0. For 0 < s < 1, the same identity becomes

0 = ∑_{k=n}^∞ a_k s^k.

Dividing by s^n and reindexing gives

0 = a_n + ∑_{j=1}^∞ a_{n+j}s^j.

Again the tail satisfies

|∑_{j=1}^∞ a_{n+j}s^j| ≤ s∑_{j=1}^∞ |a_{n+j}| ≤ 2s,

so letting s decrease to 0 gives a_n = 0. The induction is complete. Thus p_k = q_k for every nonnegative integer k, and in particular Pr(X = k) = Pr(Y = k) for every k ∈ ℕ. This proves both implications.
